A: Teacher Malcolm promised his graduating class a final weekend review before their licensing exam. On Saturday morning he wakes with laryngitis and a fever; the substitute does not know the material, yet speaking for four hours could prolong his illness. Should Malcolm conduct the review his students rely on or cancel it and recover?
B: Janelle coordinates volunteers rebuilding a wheelchair ramp for an elderly neighbor, and the concrete delivery cannot be moved. A strained back makes lifting painful, while several first-time volunteers need her hands-on direction to finish before rain arrives. Should Janelle work through the pain to meet her commitment or stay home and let her back heal?
C: Professor Wei is invited to deliver a short keynote overseas, an appearance likely to raise his profile and consulting income. The trip requires two long flights for a twenty-minute talk, despite an equally useful video option, adding emissions that contribute to a burden shared far beyond the conference. Should Wei fly for the career benefit or present remotely to limit that impact?

A: Dairy farmer Elise promised her brother she would cover the predawn milking while he attended his daughter's graduation. She develops food poisoning overnight, and no relief worker is available; leaving the herd waiting creates distress and lost production, but entering the barn while weak may worsen her condition. Should Elise complete the milking or remain in bed to recover?
B: Cellist Anton's quartet is recording the final movement today after months of shared preparation. His wrist has become swollen and numb, and the specialist warned that continued playing could turn a minor injury into lasting damage, but canceling forfeits the rented studio and everyone's work. Should Anton perform his part or withdraw to protect his hand?
C: Every winter, Lila prunes her apple trees before buds emerge, producing healthier branches and a stronger autumn crop. This mild afternoon is her last available chance, but the work is repetitive and she would rather sit by the fire with a new novel and cider. Should Lila complete the pruning or enjoy the comfortable afternoon indoors?

A: Tailor Simone has promised forty altered uniforms to a restaurant opening tomorrow. A sudden eye infection makes close stitching painful and her doctor advised avoiding detailed work, but the restaurant cannot postpone its opening and her assistant cannot finish alone. Should Simone sew through the evening to deliver the uniforms or stop and protect her eyesight?
B: Goalkeeper Pavel agreed to play in the amateur league final because his club has no reserve. After a fall at work, he has a suspected concussion and needs monitoring, yet withdrawing would force ten teammates to forfeit the match they trained all year to reach. Should Pavel honor his commitment to play or sit out for his health?
C: Bookshop owner Clara charges every vendor the same nonrefundable fee for canceling an event within forty-eight hours. A debut author cancels because her child has been hospitalized and asks Clara to return money needed for travel, although two other vendors recently paid the fee. Should Clara grant this hardship exception or apply the cancellation policy equally?

A: Marine researcher Soraya can join an exploratory voyage to an unmapped vent field where the crew may discover unknown species, but weather and sampling success are uncertain. A funded laboratory placement offers guaranteed data, a fixed schedule, and established methods, though little room for discovery. Should Soraya take the open-ended voyage or choose the predictable laboratory project?
B: Residents give Mateo a vacant lot for a summer community project. He can let volunteers improvise gardens, play areas, and gathering spaces as ideas emerge, risking unfinished work, or follow a contractor's fixed plan for a modest park with certified equipment and a guaranteed opening date. Should Mateo support the evolving volunteer design or select the dependable standard plan?
C: At her institute's annual field survey, geologist Nia wants to replace handwritten notebooks with tablets that attach coordinates and photographs to each observation. The senior team values the marked paper volumes used for fifty years and fears losing the craft of careful field notes. Should Nia introduce digital records or continue the institute's longstanding notebook tradition?

A: Climber Felix has one free day in the Dolomites and can attempt an unmarked ridge that promises new views but has uncertain rock conditions. The local guide recommends a protected route with reliable anchors and an exact descent time, though Felix has climbed it twice before. Should Felix explore the unknown ridge or take the secure familiar route?
B: Programmer Yasmin is choosing the foundation for a personal game. An experimental engine would let her invent unusual physics and perhaps produce something distinctive, but documentation is incomplete and the project may fail; a mature engine supplies tested tools and predictable results within her vacation. Should Yasmin explore the experimental engine or use the reliable established one?
C: A youth football league needs replacement goalposts before Saturday's tournament. Fabricator Hugo can weld a basic set by Friday, allowing every match to proceed, or spend another week reinforcing joints and applying weatherproof coating for a safer, longer-lasting finish. Should Hugo deliver the workable goalposts in time or delay the tournament to complete them properly?

A: After standard therapies fail, patient coordinator Lena can enroll Mr. Harris in a new trial whose benefits and side effects remain uncertain. A conventional treatment is unlikely to cure him but has a well-known course and can reliably control symptoms for months. Should Lena encourage the experimental possibility or recommend the predictable treatment plan?
B: Runner Keisha has qualified for a trail race where competitors choose their own route between mountain checkpoints, offering adventure but uncertain terrain and finish times. A road race that weekend follows closed streets, staffed aid stations, and a pace she can forecast. Should Keisha enter the open-route trail event or choose the controlled road race?
C: Pharmacist Omar notices that his longtime friend, a physician, prescribed twice the recommended dose to a child. Alerting the hospital would correct the record and protect the patient, but an investigation could end his friend's struggling practice after one mistake. Should Omar report the dosing error or shield his friend from professional harm?

A: Transit planner Evelyn can test an on-demand night bus whose route changes with passenger requests, potentially reaching isolated residents but producing uncertain wait times. Keeping the fixed loop guarantees published stops and dependable timing, although several neighborhoods remain beyond walking distance. Should Evelyn pilot the flexible service or retain the predictable fixed route?
B: For his final university term, Lucas can design an independent course around archival material nobody has catalogued, with no assurance the work will yield a coherent thesis. A standard seminar provides a proven syllabus, frequent grading, and a clear path to graduation. Should Lucas pursue the uncertain independent study or enroll in the structured seminar?
C: The town clerk wants residents to book appointments through a new online portal that could shorten queues and send automatic reminders. Older staff and many longtime residents value the walk-in counter and the numbered paper tickets used since the municipal hall opened. Should the clerk adopt online booking or preserve the familiar public-service routine?

A: A neighborhood association gives Inez funds for a riverfront mural but no final design. She can invite residents to paint whatever develops over the weekend, risking a disjointed result, or hire a studio offering an approved sketch, insured painters, and guaranteed completion. Should Inez open the wall to uncertain collaboration or commission the predictable professional design?
B: Park ranger Cole can lead visitors into a newly opened wetland where wildlife sightings and trail conditions are unpredictable. The established boardwalk tour has railings, mapped stops, and a reliable return time but reveals little beyond familiar habitats. Should Cole offer the exploratory wetland walk or keep the group on the protected boardwalk route?
C: Organizer Fatima has been invited to direct a national housing coalition, a position that could give her campaigns far greater influence. Accepting requires leaving the tenant group whose members meet in her kitchen and have shared years of victories and setbacks. Should Fatima pursue the national leadership role or remain with her close neighborhood organization?

A: Engineer Becca learns that her close friend quietly copied licensed code into the startup's new product and told managers it was original. Revealing the source prevents a false release and possible legal trouble, but her friend would likely be fired days before his wedding. Should Becca tell the managers what she found or protect her friend by staying silent?
B: Physicist Samuel reviews a paper written by his former supervisor and discovers that its strongest graph omits several measurements that contradict the conclusion. Correcting the record may trigger a retraction and damage the mentor who launched his career, while silence lets a misleading result stand. Should Samuel report the missing measurements or remain loyal to his mentor?
C: App designer Lotte prefers a quiet interface with no engagement streaks, believing users should decide when to return. Her investors and colleagues insist on daily badges and warn that rejecting them will make her seem difficult before promotion decisions. Should Lotte build the restrained product she believes in or add the features that would win the team's approval?

A: Museum registrar Celia discovers that a painting donated by her uncle has documentation proving it was taken from a family during wartime. Disclosing the records could force restitution and publicly disgrace the relative who financed her education, while concealing them preserves a false ownership history. Should Celia reveal the painting's provenance or protect her uncle's reputation?
B: Ecologist Bram realizes that his research partner and closest friend counted the same bird colony twice in a report already sent to conservation officials. Correcting the figure could cost her a grant and embarrass their lab, but leaving it unchallenged misstates the population. Should Bram notify the officials of the error or stand by his friend?
C: Choreographer Nadine has built a new dance around movements she developed during treatment for depression. Explaining that history to the company could help dancers understand the piece and invite more honest collaboration, but it would expose deeply personal medical details. Should Nadine share the origin of the dance or keep her experience private?

A: School counselor Irene learns that her colleague and friend altered a senior's attendance record so the student could graduate. Reporting the change restores an accurate transcript but may cost the colleague her job and strain a decade-long friendship; silence protects her while preserving false information. Should Irene inform the principal or remain loyal to her friend?
B: Surgeon Malik notices that his longtime operating partner documented a procedure as complication-free despite a sponge being briefly left inside the patient and removed. Correcting the chart may bring disciplinary action against someone he trusts, yet the current record hides clinically relevant truth. Should Malik amend the chart and report the incident or protect his partner?
C: Tutor Grace promised to supervise six anxious students through an overnight mathematics competition. She develops a severe asthma flare shortly before departure, and no other teacher knows the travel arrangements; canceling would end their participation, but attending means hours away from her usual clinic. Should Grace accompany the students as promised or withdraw to protect her breathing?

A: Farm inspector Alice finds that her cousin has been labeling ordinary eggs as free-range after storm damage confined the hens indoors. Recording the violation protects accurate sales information but could cancel the contract keeping his farm afloat, while overlooking it shields a relative through a difficult season. Should Alice file the truthful report or protect her cousin's livelihood?
B: Nurse Theo learns that his closest coworker changed a patient's fall time in the chart to make it appear that staffing rules were followed. Correcting the entry preserves an honest medical record but could lead to her suspension and leave her family without wages. Should Theo report the altered time or remain loyal to his coworker?
C: Young farmer Mira wants to replace part of the family wheat field with the herbs she enjoys growing and has already found local buyers. Her parents and neighboring farmers expect her to continue the crop that defines the family farm and dismiss herbs as unserious. Should Mira plant according to her own preference or keep wheat to retain their approval?
